comments.author: @breacoteen
comments.text:
good video.
you briefly mentioned demographics, but i don't think you conveyed how critical the situation is. korea's basically going to depopulate drastically. they've been trying to incentivise people to have kids, but nothing has worked.
it's a national crisis, so it needs crisis measures:
1. offer couples who have a child a MASSIVE percentage of the price of an apartment, up to a certain value, say a quarter of a million dollars.
2. by law, cut fees at hagwons (private schools that kids are sent to after their regular school hours) in half, and cap fee increases to match the rate of inflation, permanently.
3. by law, stipulate that only a certain percentage of employees (say 33%) in both the private and public sectors have studied at SKY (the three top universities). this would mean a quota at every organisation above a certain size.
(2 and 3 are vital because a massive cost of having a child in korea is the need to send them to hagwons in order to get them into one of the top universities.)
4. strengthen maternity leave laws so that women can easily go back to their jobs after having a child, and severely punish employers who break the law in this respect.
5. subsidise childcare much, much more.
there would be huge pushback against some or all of these, but half measures are no longer enough.
of course a lot of this would not be necessary if they would allow in a lot more immigrants who could over time qualify for citizenship, but as in many other countries, my sense is that a lot of koreans would rather the country dies off rather than letting this happen.

comments.author: @breacoteen
comments.text:
you're missing one big aesthetic downside of seoul, namely the massive roads that cut through the city, usually 8-lane. i think one of the reasons for their size is so that the military can move quickly and easily in the case of a north korean attack. 
the effect is the separation of adjacent parts of the city from each other, the dominance of traffic and the lack of a cosy feel to so much of the city. (thankfully, you only have to walk one block away from these major roads and very often you are in a nice neighborhood). 
if ever the north korean threat abates they should halve the width of these roads, planting trees in the now-defunct lanes, which would elevate seoul immeasurably.
